opening.headline: Dividing a document into chunks solves the problem of context loss and incorrect search results by attaching context to each chunk.
body: Retrieval-based question answering often mistakenly attributes incorrect answers to embedding models or the questions themselves. However, the root cause is frequently much earlier in the pipeline. When documents are split into smaller chunks, they lose the contextual information that would indicate which company and which time period the chunk pertains to.

In this class, we first verify how traditional RAG works and examine how context loss undermines retrieval. We then explore the principles and improvement effects of Contextual Retrieval—attaching explanatory context before each chunk—and follow along with a walkthrough of the process of repairing chunks where context has been lost.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the principle of contextual retrieval.
Search failure reasons can be differentiated into chunking and context loss, allowing for the establishment of an improvement priority order.

screens.title: A chunk loses its context and is retrieved to the wrong location.
screens.lead: Read the following scenario and consider where the true root cause of the search failure might lie.

visual.alt: A chunk whose company is unknown on its own, and a similar chunk belonging to an unrelated company placed side by side.
labels: What was ACME's quarter-two 2023 sales growth rate?
Going up to the parent level
Fourth quarter revenue decreased compared to the previous quarter.

paragraphs: There is a service that uses publicly disclosed company filings as its search target. A user asks about ACME's revenue growth rate in the second quarter of 2023. The sentence containing the correct answer states: "The company's revenue increased by 3% compared to the previous quarter."

Reading this sentence in isolation does not reveal which company or time period it refers to. The search system looks for chunks of text that are semantically or lexically close to the query, but these chunks contain neither the company name nor the time period mentioned in the query. As a result, it may instead rank sentences from other companies that are similar, placing them higher in the results.

Dividing a document into small pieces makes searching faster and cheaper, but each piece loses surrounding context. This course confirms that context loss is a common cause of search failures and addresses solutions to this problem.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Will making chunks larger solve the problem or create a new one? This question is addressed in the considerations for implementing the lesson.

screens.outro: First, let's consider where we would look for the cause when a search fails.

screens.title: Recalling the experience of identifying search failure reasons within a chinking context
screens.lead: When a candidate is selected, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Since no answer is entered or submitted, first think about it in relation to your own experience.

items.prompt: Have you ever thought that your embedding model was weak and caused the search to fail?
items.answer: This is a common initial suspicion. However, if the chunk itself remains ambiguous even when switching to a different embedding model, improvements are limited. In Anthropic's experiments, the technique of adding context improved performance across all tested combinations of embedding models. The correct sequence is to first examine the chunk before changing the model.

items.prompt: Have you ever thought that a query was ambiguous and thus search failed?
items.answer: There are indeed issues with question-related content. However, if a wrong chunk appears despite the question being clearly defined, the chunk itself should be suspected. A typical example is when the question includes both company name and period, but the correct chunk lacks both.

items.prompt: Has the retrieved chunk previously failed to be read independently?
items.answer: This is the simplest and most certain diagnosis. Take one answer chunk from a failed search and read it in isolation. If you cannot determine what topic it relates to within a document, the likelihood is high that context loss is the cause.

screens.outro: We will verify the chunking and retrieval process of traditional RAG using a structural diagram.

screens.title: Traditional RAG flow and chunking
screens.lead: When you select the number marker on the diagram, you can view the role of each step. Please check them in order from step 1.

visual.alt: The document is divided into chunks and stored using embedding and BM25 indexing; when a query comes in, results retrieved through both methods are combined, and the top K results are appended to the prompt.
labels: Generate based on the prompt attached

markers.label: Chunk segmentation
markers.title: Chunking: dividing a document into smaller parts
markers.body: The knowledge base is typically divided into chunks of fewer than hundreds of tokens. Smaller chunks enable faster search and reduce the amount of text appended to the prompt. When the document corpus exceeds the context window, this approach becomes a common solution. The size of chunks, their boundaries, and overlap levels affect search performance. At this stage, chunks become decoupled from the overall context of the document.

markers.label: Embedding
markers.title: Embedding Generation: Converts meaning into numbers
markers.body: The embedding model converts each chunk into a vector that captures its meaning and stores it in a vector database. When a question is posed, it can find chunks with similar meaning. While embedding effectively captures semantic relationships, it may miss exact string matches.

markers.label: BM25 Index
markers.title: BM25 indexing: indexing for word matching
markers.body: BM25 ranks documents based on whether words or phrases match exactly, taking document length into account and correcting for common words that might otherwise dominate results. It performs well in queries containing unique identifiers or technical terminology, such as error code TS-999. While embeddings may retrieve general information about error codes, BM25 helps compensate for the risk of missing the exact TS-999 document.

markers.label: search for meaning
markers.title: Embedding similarity search
markers.body: Queries are also converted into vectors using the same embedding model, and similar chunks are retrieved based on meaning. The advantage is that even with different keywords, semantically similar chunks can be retrieved. This follows the same principle as semantic search in OpenAI Search.

markers.label: Word search
markers.title: BM25 Term Matching Search
markers.body: It searches for chunks based on whether the words in the question appear exactly within the chunks. It enforces exact string matching. Conversely, if a word from the question does not exist in a chunk, there is no match. This aspect connects to the context loss problem in the next screen.

markers.label: Combine ranks
markers.title: Ranking combination and top K selection
markers.body: The results from both methods are combined using a ranking fusion technique, duplicates are removed, and the top K chunks are appended to the prompt. Experimental results show that using both embeddings and BM25 performs better than using embeddings alone. Google's RAG setup and OpenAI search also follow this approach of segmentation, embedding, indexing, and search.

screens.outro: As an example, let's look at how context is lost in this structure.

screens.title: How context loss undermines search
screens.lead: Alternate between the two state buttons to compare how search engines treat a chunk with context attached versus a chunk with context appended immediately after splitting.

states.label: Chunk after split
states.body: The chunk content states that the company's revenue increased by 3% compared to the previous quarter. At the moment of splitting, a chunk is separated from surrounding information such as document title, company name, and period. Embedding generates meaning based solely on the chunk itself, thus not reflecting which company it pertains to. BM25 will not match if the word "ACME" appears in the query but is absent from the chunk. As a result, similar sentences from other companies may appear at the top of results. Whether the issue stems from chunking or from the model can be distinguished by reading the chunk independently. This problem becomes more severe when documents are long and contain many sections with similar formatting—for example, when consolidated financial disclosures from different companies are accumulated. Similar sentences within chunks make it difficult to distinguish between them. The impact is minimal when documents are short and each chunk already contains the core subject.

states.label: Contextualized chunk
states.body: This chunk is annotated with a description from ACME's second-quarter 2023 SEC filing, stating that revenue in the prior quarter was $314 million. Now, in embedding, the meaning of company and period is captured, and the term "ACME" is indexed in BM25. Since both methods connect questions and chunks, the correct chunk ranks higher. The attached context is typically a brief explanation of 50 to 100 tokens. The article notes that attaching general document summaries to chunks provides very limited benefit. The key point is that the context is per-chunk, explaining what this specific chunk represents within the document, rather than summarizing the entire document. Even if chunks come from the same document, their contexts must differ.

screens.outro: We will examine the methods of context attachment and verify their effectiveness with numbers.

screens.title: Contextual Retrieval: Attach context to chunks
screens.lead: When you move the slider to add techniques one by one, check how the ratio of failing to find relevant documents within the top 20 chunks decreases.

visual.alt: Bar chart showing search failure rate decreasing from 5.7% to 1.9% as more techniques are added.
labels: Failure rate of top 20 chunk search (%)

stops.body: A traditional setup that combines embedding and BM25. The failure rate, defined as the proportion of top 20 chunks that do not retrieve relevant documents, is 5.7%. This value serves as the baseline for comparison. Performance improvements from re-ranking can be verified using the same question set.

After attaching a brief context explaining each chunk, we create embeddings. The retrieval failure rate decreased from 5.7% to 3.7%, representing a reduction of approximately 35%. The context is generated by prompting the model to show it the entire document and the chunk, and then to write a short description explaining how this chunk fits within the document.

We build a BM25 index using context-aware chunks. This reduces the search failure rate from 2.9%, resulting in a roughly 49% decrease. These two sub-techniques are Contextual Embeddings and Contextual BM25. The results also align with the finding that combining embeddings with BM25 performs better than using embeddings alone.

After retrieving approximately the top 150 results initially, a re-ranking model rescores them based on their relevance to the query, ultimately selecting the top 20. The search failure rate has dropped to 1.9%, representing a reduction of about 67%. Re-ranking introduces an additional step at execution time, causing a slight increase in latency and cost. While performance improves with more chunks being re-ranked, latency and cost also increase, so a balance must be experimentally determined.

screens.outro: Let's apply this technique to a single chunk without context.

screens.title: Chunk explanation without context
screens.lead: We'll walk through the process of fixing a chunk with lost context. Select the arrow and proceed step by step, following the improvement order.

steps.title: Problem chunk: The company's revenue increased by 3%.
steps.body: Assume there is a relevant chunk that does not rank in the top results. The content of this chunk states that the company's revenue increased by 3% compared to the prior quarter. The user asked about ACME's revenue growth in the second quarter of 2023, but this chunk did not appear in the top 20 results.

steps.title: Step 1. Diagnosis: Read the chip independently
steps.body: If you simply extract and read a chunk, you won't be able to determine which company or which period it refers to. This confirms that the issue stems from context loss, not from the choice of embedding model or the nature of the question. By verifying chunks before switching models, you can significantly reduce costs.

steps.title: Step 2. Contextualization
steps.body: Show the entire document and its chunks to the model, and instruct it to write a short description placing the chunk within the document. For example, this chunk comes from ACME's Q2 2023 SEC filing and states that revenue in the prior quarter was $314 million. Attach this description before the chunk. Humans cannot annotate hundreds of thousands of chunks, so the model generates these annotations.

steps.title: Step 3. Rescanning
steps.body: Both embedding and BM25 indexing are recreated using context-aware chunks. If only one of them is rebuilt, the effectiveness is halved. When documents are large, you can significantly reduce context generation costs by loading the document once using prompt caching and reusing it across chunks. The text assumes a one-time cost of $1.02 per million document tokens.

steps.title: Step 4. Quality Verification
steps.body: We create a question set to compare the ratio of relevant chunks appearing within the top K results before and after improvement. The document metric is the proportion of documents missed within the top 20. Chunk boundaries, embedding model, context generation prompt, and number of chunks to retrieve all influence the results, so evaluations are repeated to establish reliability.

screens.outro: Summarize the key points at the final screen.

screens.title: Chunks need to be accompanied by context.
screens.lead: This lesson's key points are summarized. Please review your answers to the questions posed in the problem presentation screen.

paragraphs: Chinking sacrifices context for speed and cost. When a search result is incorrect, before doubting the model, read the correct chunk independently. Contextual Retrieval attaches explanatory context before each chunk to generate embeddings and BM25, thereby mitigating this loss.

Going back to the first question, simply increasing chunk size is insufficient. As chunks grow larger, unrelated content increases, leading to additional issues. Attaching context provides a more direct solution, and its effectiveness can be verified through before-and-after comparisons of the question set. Additionally, the number of chunks retrieved can be adjusted. While comparing 5, 10, and 20 chunks, 20 showed the best results; however, too much information may overwhelm the model, so experimentation with my own data is necessary.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: The reduction rate in the text is the average result measured by Anthropic across multiple knowledge domains. Verify it again using my question set in your data.

checks.intro: Just now, recall the principle of context loss and verify it for yourself. The result is not recorded.
checks.q: The chunk "That company's revenue increased by 3%" was ranked lower than a more appropriate chunk in response to the question "What is ACME's revenue growth rate?" What is the most likely reason?
options: The model is too small to read numbers
The chunk is too long to be embedded.
As it is split, company names and other surrounding information are lost, making it impossible to connect with ACME via embedding or BM25.
BM25 does not support indexing numbers.
checks.explain: If a chunk is separated from the document title, company, and period, embedding will only consider the chunk to derive meaning, while BM25 will not match because there are no words from the query.

wrong.0: The cause is not the model but loss of contextual information during tokenization.
wrong.1: Chunks are typically shorter than a few hundred tokens.
wrong.3: BM25 is strong in exact word matching, but the problem is that the words from the query may not appear in the chunks.

checks.intro: Recall the improvement process just explained and arrange it appropriately. The result is not recorded.
checks.q: Try arranging the steps to fix chunks that have lost their context.
items: Checks independently whether reading a chunk results in context loss.
Attach contextual information such as document title, company, and quarter to the beginning of each chunk.
Rebuilds the embedding and BM25 indexing using a appended chunk.
Compares the ratio of related chunks appearing within the top K items in a question set.
checks.explain: Diagnosis, context assignment, re-indexing, and quality verification in this order. The chunks must be remade using the combined embeddings and BM25.

glossary.def: This involves dividing a document into small pieces based on search units.
This is a phenomenon where a fragment loses surrounding information such as the original title, subject, and period, becoming isolated and ambiguous.
This is a search optimization technique that attaches explanatory context before chunks to create embeddings and BM25 indexing.
A search ranking method based on word matching. Strong in exact string search.

misconceptions.myth: If the search is wrong, it's the fault of the embedding model.
misconceptions.fact: It is common for chunks to not be read independently. You can determine this by reading a chunk independently before switching models.

misconceptions.myth: Make the chunk larger and it will be solved.
misconceptions.fact: Increasing chunk size can lead to issues such as irrelevant content appearing. Attaching context directly to each chunk is a more straightforward solution.

misconceptions.myth: Fix it once and that's it.
misconceptions.fact: You need to compare the failure rate of search before and after using a question set. Since results may vary depending on chunk boundaries and embedding models, evaluations should be repeated.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Chinking increases speed but causes context loss, leading to search failures.
Contextual Retrieval reduced search failures by 49% on its own, and by 67% when combined with re-ranking.
Search quality is verified through before-and-after comparisons of question sets.
